source.title: Experience-Driven Multi-Agent Optimization for Black-Box Jailbreak Attacks on Large Language Models
source.authors: Zhaoyang Han; Yihe Liu; Kai Zhang; Ping Li

record.tranche_reason: The paper develops and evaluates its own black-box jailbreak attack method. It reports attack success, but does not test fine-tuning, token-position KL, compliant prefilling, suffix or decoding bypasses, or safety localization.
record.gate_note: The reported ASR results measure harmful compliance deliberately induced by EMJO adversarial prompts. They do not establish that models comply without that inducement or test the listed claim mechanisms. Comparator-only baseline results and AQC results are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes a black-box multi-agent jailbreak prompt optimizer (EMJO) and reports only its own attack success and query efficiency against baselines. It uses no fine-tuning (V1, V2), measures no per-token KL (V3), and does not test prefilling, suffixes or decoding changes (V4). It also does not localize parameters (V5), test causes of shallowness (V6), or test deepening training (V7). The ASRs measure deliberately induced compliance from the authors' own method.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: the authors conclude EMJO outperforms black-box jailbreak baselines in ASR and query efficiency, transfers across backbones, and that experience reuse helps solve previously failed queries, especially on strongly aligned models.
record.recipe_differences: A black-box multi-agent adversarial-prompt optimization framework evaluated by attack success rate; it does not use fine-tuning or measure token-position KL, compliant prefilling, suffixes, or decoding changes.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by target model and dataset. The paper also reports that Llama-Guard lowers ASR and raises AQC, and that StrongREJECT yields a lower ASR than the original evaluation protocol.

fits_no_version.finding: EMJO's iteratively optimized semantic jailbreak prompts reach 76–100% judged ASR on AdvBench subset and 80–94.55% on JailbreakBench across five target models. ASR drops to 76.36% under StrongREJECT and 80% behind a Llama-Guard filter (DeepSeek-V3 target).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Black-box multi-agent prompt optimization with an experience memory elicits judged harmful compliance from safety-aligned chat models within a few queries.

record.peer_reviewed: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2026
record.problems: The study says it focuses primarily on English queries and prompts. Its main ASR evaluation uses DeepSeek-V3 as a reference judge; under the stricter StrongREJECT assessment, reported ASR is lower. No uncertainty estimates are reported in the shown tables.
record.rows_left_out: Comparator-only baseline ASR results in Tables 1, 2, 4, and 5 are omitted because they compare jailbreak methods rather than test a listed claim version. Table 3 component ablations are omitted because they compare variants of the paper's own method. Figure 2 backbone comparisons, Figure 3 iteration trends, Figure 4 failure-recovery results, and AQC results beyond the defense condition are omitted because they report the method's performance or efficiency, not a listed claim version.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, adversarial suffix or decoding manipulation; only semantic prompt rewriting (role-play, obfuscation, encoding) is used.
No data or objective explanation is tested.

record.verdict_notes: The record's T4/uses_without_test classification is right. The paper cites Qi et al. 2024 (an original source) only as a white-box attack reference. Baseline TAP is described as exploring 'adversarial suffixes', but neither TAP nor EMJO tests V4's mechanism of getting past the opening tokens. Target generations were capped at 150 tokens, and the main judge is DeepSeek-V3, which is also the attacker backbone and one of the targets.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning and its effect on refusal.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.
The paper tests its own adversarial prompt attacks, not whether compliant prefilling, adversarial suffixes, decoding changes, or getting past initial response tokens bypass safety.
No weights or ranks are localized, edited, or ablated for safety.
No data or training-objective explanation of safety shallowness is tested.
No training intended to deepen safety behavior is tested.
